request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:
Admitting Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
A 60-year-old female presented to the emergency room with a sudden onset of severe headache associated with vomiting. On the administration of a CT scan of the brain, subarachnoid hemorrhage was observed, and an aneurysm was suspected. The patient underwent CT cerebral angiogram, and a bilobed anterior communicating artery aneurysm was discovered, projecting anterosuperiorly with a size of 8 x 7 x 5 mm. On the fourth day of ictus, the patient underwent right pterional craniotomy and clipping of the aneurysm. Following surgery, the patient developed right-sided ptosis that advanced to complete right-sided oculomotor nerve paralysis with a dilated and nonreacting pupil. A CT scan of the brain was performed, but no hematoma or infarct was noted. The patient was discharged on the eighth postoperative day and kept under regular follow-up in our outpatient department.

Discharge Condition:
Stable with recovered oculomotor nerve paralysis.

Course of Treatment:
The patient was administered antiedema measures, anticonvulsant, analgesic, and Nimodipine. The medication was continued for a total of 21 days following the ictus.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with their healthcare provider regularly.

Follow-up Care:
The patient underwent a Magnetic Resonance Imaging scan of the brain with venogram to rule out any infarct or thrombosis of the cavernous sinus after a week of discharge. No abnormalities were noted. The patient came for follow-up on the 61st postoperative day, and her ptosis had fully recovered. A full recovery of the ocular motor nerve paralysis was noted. The patient was advised to continue regular follow-up with their healthcare provider.

Discharge Medications:
Medications are not listed as per case report instructions.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The condition chiefly responsible for the admission is a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm causing subarachnoid hemorrhage. In ICD-10, I60 covers subarachnoid hemorrhage, and I60.2 is specifically "from anterior communicating artery". A ruptured berry aneurysm is classified to I60, not I67.1 (unruptured cerebral aneurysm).

The postoperative oculomotor nerve palsy is a complication, so it would be coded as a secondary diagnosis and not the principal one.

CODE: I60
